claim: TikTok's own commissioned report 'The TikTok Effect' (published 15 June 2023) contains a 9-country chart showing the percentage of surveyed creators earning more than minimum wage on TikTok, and coordinate-level reconstruction of the chart (matched against the report's own footnote pinning Myanmar to n=26 low-base) resolves Indonesia's value as 63% -- meaning the 63%-above-minimum-wage figure IS traceable to a disclosed primary survey, contrary to the assumption that it is a wholly unsourced number.
stance_target: the claim that Indonesia's 63%-above-minimum-wage figure has no traceable underlying methodology whatsoever
scope_conditions: The raw PDF text-extraction stream scrambles the chart's number-to-label order; the pairing used here is derived from x/y coordinate proximity of each text run on the page (via PyMuPDF), and is corroborated by an independent check: the resulting Myanmar=73%* pairing exactly matches the report's separately stated footnote 'Low base (<n=30): Myanmar (n=26)', giving confidence the coordinate-based reconstruction is correct
quoted_support: Percentage of surveyed creators earning more than minimum wage on TikTok in SEA [chart values by coordinate-matched country: Indonesia 63%, Vietnam 83%, Laos 87%, Cambodia 56%, Myanmar 73%*, Thailand 36%, Malaysia 80%, Singapore 68%, The Philippines 40%] ... *Low base (<n=30): Myanmar (n=26)
time_period: Survey fielded August-September 2022; report published 15 June 2023

claim: The report's Methodology addendum discloses Indonesia's TOTAL quantitative survey sample as n=540 (250 main-city + 290 secondary-city respondents), but this is the base for the general TikTok-user survey, NOT the specific sub-base of 'creators who use TikTok as a source of income' over which the 63% figure is computed -- that income-earner sub-n is never disclosed per country anywhere in the report.
stance_target: the 63% figure, while traceable, still lacks a fully disclosed denominator and should not be treated as methodologically complete
scope_conditions: Addendum table gives per-country total samples for the general quantitative survey (N=3,412 across 9 markets); it does not break down samples by respondent sub-type (e.g., creators vs. SMB owners vs. general users vs. educators) per country
quoted_support: Market Indonesia: Main Cities n=250, Secondary Cities n=290, Total Sample n=540 ... Among polled creators who use TikTok as a source of income, most are earning more than the minimum wage in their respective nations, according to our survey data.

claim: The '8 million creators' population figure attributed to TikTok Indonesia and Menekraf Harsya does not appear anywhere in the 36-page 'The TikTok Effect' report -- the report contains only percentages among survey respondents (rates, not counts), never a national or platform-wide creator headcount for any of the 9 countries surveyed.
stance_target: the 8-million-creators figure traces to TikTok's own commissioned SEA impact study
scope_conditions: Audited absence across the full report text (7,847 words, 36 pages) including the methodology addendum and glossary; no population estimates, extrapolations, or headcounts of any kind are present in the document
quoted_support: In SEA, more than 80% of TikTok creators have boosted their incomes through multiple avenues, such as earning through TikTok LIVE or working with brands through paid sponsorships, according to our regional survey. Among polled creators who use TikTok as a source of income, most are earning more than the minimum wage in their respective nations, according to our survey data.

claim: The minimum-wage benchmark used to compute Indonesia's 63% figure is a single national value of USD 216/month sourced to 'ASEAN Briefing,' which collapses Indonesia's substantial province-by-province UMR (Upah Minimum Regional) variation into one number -- the same simplification the pipeline flagged when the figure was repeated by Menekraf Harsya without an internal source.
stance_target: even the traceable version of the 63% figure inherits a real methodological simplification about which minimum wage was used
scope_conditions: Footnote-level disclosure only; the report does not explain whether respondents were asked about their own provincial minimum wage or compared uniformly against the national figure
quoted_support: Minimum wages (in USD) for SEA markets fielded are as follows: Malaysia (279), Vietnam (158), Laos (116), Philippines (177), Myanmar (61), Singapore (2078), Indonesia (216), Cambodia (192), Thailand (208).
numbers: Singapore USD 2,078 (living-wage proxy, not a legal minimum wage)
entities: Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy (LKYSPP)

claim: The underlying survey sample is a self-selected convenience sample of existing, active TikTok users recruited by or through TikTok/Kadence -- not a random or representative sample of all creators or all residents of each country -- meaning even the traceable 63% figure is subject to the same survivorship/self-selection bias that affects nearly all platform-commissioned creator-income studies.
stance_target: survivorship bias inflates reported creator income/success rates across the literature, including this SEA-specific study
scope_conditions: Inferred from the disclosed methodology (online survey of TikTok users plus offline interviews in three developing markets); no sampling frame, response rate, or recruitment-channel detail beyond 'TikTok users' is disclosed
quoted_support: On behalf of TikTok, Kadence International conducted this survey to explore the impact of TikTok across SEA. It was conducted across nine SEA markets and included more than 3,400 TikTok users and 25 non-profit organizations and ran between August and September 2022.

claim: In SEA overall, 'more than 80% of TikTok creators have boosted their incomes through multiple avenues, such as earning through TikTok LIVE or working with brands through paid sponsorships,' and 93% of SEA creators surveyed believed TikTok is a platform where they can monetize their skills -- both regional aggregates distinct from the country-specific minimum-wage chart.
stance_target: TikTok is broadly perceived by its own self-selected surveyed creator base in SEA as a viable income source
scope_conditions: Regional 9-country aggregate, not country-specific; self-selected TikTok-user sample; 'boosted their incomes' does not establish absolute income level or living-wage adequacy, only a self-reported directional increase
quoted_support: In SEA, more than 80% of TikTok creators have boosted their incomes through multiple avenues, such as earning through TikTok LIVE or working with brands through paid sponsorships, according to our regional survey. ... 93% of SEA creators believed TikTok is a platform where they can monetize their skills
